title: Taiwan Moves to Make Unlicensed AI Chip Exports to China a Crime
dek: A Foreign Trade Act amendment heard in Taiwan's legislature would impose up to 10 years in prison for shipping listed chips, materials or tools to China, including through third countries.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: A large TSMC factory building in Hsinchu, Taiwan

keyPoints: Taiwan's Legislative Yuan Economics Committee held a public hearing on Monday, November 2, on a Foreign Trade Act amendment proposed by DPP lawmakers.

The bill would require government approval to export listed integrated circuits, wafer materials, parts and fabrication equipment to mainland China, and would cover goods routed through third countries.
Proposed penalties include up to 10 years in prison and fines of up to NT$10 million, with illegal profits confiscated, per Taiwan News and Asia Times.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs backed the amendment; the bill follows an August indictment over 74 Supermicro servers with Nvidia GPUs allegedly sent to China.
body:
Taiwan is moving to turn unauthorized exports of advanced chips to China into a criminal offense, a step that would close a gap prosecutors ran into in a high-profile server diversion case.

## What the amendment would do

At a public hearing on Monday, the Economics Committee of the Legislative Yuan discussed a Trade Act amendment that would ban exports of certain integrated circuits, along with key wafer materials, parts and manufacturing equipment, to mainland China without government approval. According to [Taiwan News](https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/news/6470981), the current law covers only 12 categories of wafer fabrication equipment, which lawmakers say is too narrow.

The proposal also includes an anti-circumvention clause aimed at shipments that pass through third countries. [Asia Times](https://asiatimes.com/2026/11/taiwan-to-criminalize-nvidia-ai-chip-smuggling-to-china/) reports that the same penalties would apply to anyone shipping controlled goods to China through a third country, and that illegal gains would be confiscated.

## Why lawmakers acted now

The bill follows the August indictment in Keelung of nine people for allegedly exporting 74 Supermicro servers equipped with Nvidia GPUs to China. Asia Times reports that the servers reached Chinese buyers through routes that included Indonesia, Japan and Hong Kong. Taiwan News reports that employees of the two American companies were among those charged.

Asia Times notes a legal wrinkle in that case: prosecutors relied on breach of trust and document forgery under the Criminal Code, because Taiwanese law did not clearly treat the sales as an export violation. Selling to China broke the companies' internal rules and US export curbs, but not Taiwan's own export law. The amendment is meant to fill that gap.

## Government position

The Ministry of Economic Affairs backed the amendment, saying it would strengthen coordination with the United States on export controls. Taiwan is already subject to US rules under the Foreign Direct Product Rule, which extends US controls to chips made abroad with American technology. According to [CHOSUNBIZ](https://biz.chosun.com/en/en-international/2026/11/02/4SMMTNAESRHNTM3RO6WBBRIGII/), the ministry also said it was studying a wider package of measures for high-end chips.

## What is not yet known

This is a proposal before a committee, not a passed law, and no final text or vote date was reported in the coverage reviewed here. Taiwan News reported that TSMC representatives attended the hearing but did not speak. The coverage does not describe any response from Nvidia or Supermicro to the amendment.

## Market read

A tighter Taiwanese regime could raise compliance costs for distributors and server builders that handle Nvidia hardware in the region. The direct effect on Nvidia's revenue is not quantified in the reporting, so the stock read is indirect and low-confidence.
